approved_users.grain: One person who may sign in. This is the authentication table: the product does not use Supabase Auth for its own users, so a row here IS an account — credential, role, tenant and profile in one.

governance.note: READ THE POLICIES BEFORE TRUSTING THIS ROW. The table carries two policies and they contradict each other: "Users can check their own login credentials" is `FOR SELECT USING (true)`, and "No direct access - use RPCs" is `FOR ALL TO authenticated, anon USING (false)`. Postgres policies are PERMISSIVE unless declared RESTRICTIVE, and permissive policies are OR'd — so the deny-all does not deny anything, and the intended rule ("no direct access") is not the enforced one. Whether that is reachable depends on the table GRANTs Supabase applies outside `supabase/migrations/`, which no static replay can see and which PLAN.md §15 is the way to settle. Recorded as D28 and assigned to WP 2.4, which owns the RESTRICTIVE-policy decision for the whole schema; it is named here because a reader of this page must not take `rls_enabled: true` for "reads are restricted".

A row whose text org matches no organization — `'default_org'`, or a tenant renamed and re-typed — stays NULL and keeps working on the text branch. How many is a §15 question; no work-package session can reach the database.

approved_users.note: The table WP 1.4 found existed in production but in no migration — the authentication table, untracked for a year, discovered by the orphan rule (D4). `20250815000000_approved_users_base.sql` now builds it on a fresh database, and the parts of that file which are reconstruction rather than evidence are marked as such in it. This sidecar describes the table as the migrations now define it.

audit_logs.grain: One recorded action, on one plane. `admin` is what a super admin did, `data` is a tier transition — a write to tier 2, 3 or 4 — and `access` is a governed decision such as an export being allowed or refused.

governance.note: Two SELECT policies, and they are PERMISSIVE on purpose. A super admin reads every plane; an admin of the SAME ORGANIZATION as the actor reads that org's `data` and `access` rows. They grant DISJOINT slices, so the OR that D28 makes unavoidable is the intended union here rather than an accidental escape hatch — which is worth stating, because the same shape on `approved_users` IS the defect. There is no write policy: rows arrive from SECURITY DEFINER functions and from statement-level triggers, never from a client, so RLS denying writes by default is the enforcement (WP 2.2's pattern). `audited: false` on the audit table is not a joke — nothing records reads of it, and a deletion would leave no trace. Tamper-evidence is a Phase 4 question (hash-chaining a log is the same machinery as `input-hash`), not a WP 2.3 one.

policies.name: audit: org admins read their own org's data and access rows
policies.using: plane IN ('data','access') AND EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.approved_users me JOIN public.approved_users actor ON actor.id = audit_logs.actor_user_id WHERE me.id = public.get_current_user_id() AND me.role = 'admin'::public.app_role AND me.organization_id IS NOT NULL AND me.organization_id = actor.organization_id )
policies.with_check: plane IN ('data','access') AND EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.approved_users me JOIN public.approved_users actor ON actor.id = audit_logs.actor_user_id WHERE me.id = public.get_current_user_id() AND me.role = 'admin'::public.app_role AND me.organization_id IS NOT NULL AND me.organization_id = actor.organization_id )

columns.meaning: The row's identity. Returned by the emit functions so a caller can cite what it wrote.

columns.name: actor_user_id
columns.meaning: Who did it. NULLABLE, and the null carries meaning: a service-role write with no session context has no attributable actor.
columns.note: THE HONEST LIMIT OF THIS TABLE. `audit_tier_write()` reads `get_current_user_id()`, which resolves only when the caller set `app.current_user_id`. The ingest and ETL edge functions run as the service role and do not, so their rows say WHAT changed and WHEN and record `actor_known: false` in `after` rather than inventing a WHO. That is worth having and it is not attribution; closing it means those functions setting user context, which is their change to make (§16, WP 2.3).

columns.name: action
columns.meaning: What happened. Admin-plane rows use the existing dotted vocabulary (`org.update`, `api_key.revoke`); data-plane rows use the SQL operation (`insert`, `update`, `delete`); access-plane rows use `export.allowed` / `export.refused`. Three vocabularies in one column, which is a cost of one table and is recorded here rather than discovered by a reader.

columns.meaning: What kind of thing was acted on — a table name on the data plane, an entity name on the others.

columns.name: target_id
columns.meaning: Which one, as text. NULL on data-plane rows: a statement-level trigger records a STATEMENT, and a statement that touched 5,000 rows has no single id.

columns.name: before
columns.meaning: The prior state, where the writer knows it. Admin RPCs capture it; data-plane trigger rows do NOT — a statement-level trigger has the transition tables but writing 5,000 prior rows into one jsonb would make the log unreadable and unbounded. Their row COUNT is in `after` instead.

columns.name: after
columns.meaning: The resulting state, or — on a data-plane row — the shape of the statement: `tier`, `rows_after`, `rows_before` and `actor_known`. On an access-plane row it carries the decision and what was asked for.

columns.name: ip
columns.meaning: Caller IP where the writer recorded one. Never set by the triggers, which run inside the database.

columns.name: user_agent
columns.meaning: Caller user agent where the writer recorded one. As with `ip`, absent on trigger-written rows.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When it happened. Server-stamped, and the column the plane index orders by.

columns.name: plane
columns.meaning: Which plane the action belongs to — `admin`, `data` or `access`, CHECK-constrained. Added by WP 2.3; every row that predates it is `admin` by construction, because the only writer was `log_admin_action()`, which refuses anyone who is not a super admin.

substitutions.when: a row is written without naming a plane
substitutions.visible_as: the column default, which is also what makes the `admin_audit_logs` compatibility view writable for callers that have not moved yet

audit_logs.note: Coverage on the data plane is by TRIGGER, not by instrumented RPCs, and the difference is the point. WP 2.3's gap check measured 22 live SQL functions writing tier 2/3/4 with none emitting an audit row, plus six more write paths in edge functions running as the service role. Editing the 22 would have been the obvious reading of "emit on every tier transition" and would have missed all six, and would have missed the twenty-third function somebody writes next month. A statement-level trigger on each of the twelve tier 2/3/4 tables catches every writer that exists and every writer added later.

capabilities.grain: One thing a user may or may not be permitted to do — a page they may open or a feature they may use. The CATALOG: it says what rights exist, never who holds them. The four grant tables answer that.

columns.meaning: The capability's identity, and the string every grant table and every call site names. Page keys are ROUTES (`/policies`); feature keys are snake_case verbs (`data_edit_inputs`). The convention is not enforced by a CHECK.

columns.meaning: `page` or `feature`, CHECK-constrained. The resolver aggregates the two separately and returns them under separate keys, so the distinction is load-bearing rather than descriptive.

capabilities.note: THE CATALOG IS DUPLICATED IN TYPESCRIPT. `src/lib/capabilities.ts` carries the same keys as a union type and a list, because the client needs them without a round trip. Two hand-maintained copies of one fact is an I1 violation waiting to drift — `projectMembership.test.ts` asserts the WP 2.2 keys agree, but nothing checks the whole catalog, and the honest count is that the DB has grown keys the TS list learned about only when someone noticed. The contract reads narrower than the database, which is the exact class §9 asks this package to find. It is pinned by `governanceEnforcement.test.ts` rather than silently fixed: the app runs AS anon with no auth session, so revoking is a Phase 3 migration with an auth model behind it, and the decision taken was to document. delegation_grants.grain: One temporary, subtractive grant of project access from one person to another. `subtractive-delegation` (§2.1 G3) made real: a grant may never exceed what the grantor holds, and it always ends.

governance.note: `write: null` again literal. SELECT is limited to the grantor, the grantee and super admins; there is NO write policy, so RLS denies writes and `grant_project_delegation()` / `revoke_project_delegation()` are the only way in. That is forced rather than chosen: subtraction has to be CHECKED against the grantor's own level, and a PERMISSIVE policy cannot subtract (D28) — it can only add another OR'd way to say yes. `audited: false` is the uncomfortable one: a privilege grant that writes no audit row is exactly what `audit-actor` (§2.1 G4) exists to prevent, and WP 2.3 owns it. Recorded here rather than left to be noticed.

columns.meaning: When it was withdrawn early, if it was. Revocation SETS this rather than deleting the row — who held what, and when, survives the withdrawal.

delegation_grants.note: Expiry and revocation are both applied inside `effective_project_role()` rather than by each caller, so "did you remember to check expires_at" is not a question any future reader has to answer. Verified against a live PostgreSQL in WP 2.2: a grant exceeding the grantor's level is rejected, one with no expiry is rejected, and a grant whose expiry passes stops granting (PLAN.md §16).

organizations.grain: One tenant. Every project, every dataset and every simulation result in the product belongs to exactly one of these rows, and the boundary between two of them is the boundary the whole access layer is built to hold.

This is one of the few tables where `audited: true` is literally true today — WP 2.3 is what makes the claim general. Read is open to any member of the org via the self-bridge policy below, which WP 2.1 rewrote: it matched the caller's TEXT org against `name` or `slug`, so renaming an organization revoked its own members' read on the row that had just been renamed. It now bridges on `id` first.

products.grain: One finished product in one project: the economics and the demand shape the simulation reads for it. Where this row is silent the engine derives price and demand from the outbound arcs.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction. As with materials.cost, the demand-weighted outbound mean is a visible substitution, not an estimate.

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. This is the canonical G4 field: unset, the engine invents max(2 x demand, 1000), which is chosen so the constraint never binds. Estimating it from output would do the same thing with more ceremony — output is bounded by demand, so the fitted capacity can never explain a shortage.

engine_requirement.reason: With no capacity source the engine defaults to max(2·demand, 1000), so plant capacity never binds.

project_members.grain: One person's standing on one project. This is the level of access the platform did not have until WP 2.2 — between "in the organization" (sees every project) and "not in it" (sees none).

governance.note: `write: null` is LITERAL and load-bearing. The table has a SELECT policy and NO insert/update/delete policy, so RLS denies writes by default and the SECURITY DEFINER RPCs are the only way in. That is not an oversight to be tidied up later: D28 says every policy here is PERMISSIVE and permissive policies OR, so a "deny writes" policy added beside anything else would deny nothing. projects.grain: One modelling project: a named supply chain, owned by one modeller, belonging to one organization. It is the scope every other project-scoped table hangs off `project_id`, and it is the row almost every RLS policy in the schema reaches through to decide whether the caller may see anything at all.

governance.note: Tier G rather than a data tier: `projects` holds no measured quantity. It is the SCOPE, and its access rules are the ones every other table inherits by joining to it — which is why WP 2.1 had to redefine 58 policies on 24 other tables to change one comparison. Read is org-wide (any member of the owning organization sees every project in it); write is restricted to the project's own modeller or a global `admin`. There is no project-level role between those two — a member cannot be given read on one project and not another, which is `subtractive-delegation` (§2.1 G3) having nowhere to attach. WP 2.2's `project_members` is where `min_project_role: editor` above stops being a forward declaration. `audited: false`: project creation and deletion write no audit row (WP 2.3).

risk_data.note: The second of WP 1.4's three orphans (D4), and the one that turned out not to be an orphan at all. Two network pages read it and no migration created it — but the table EXISTS in the production database, untracked, with the spreadsheet-header columns `COUNTRY` and `"RISK CLASS"`. CI proved it: the first version of the migration was a plain `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, which no-opped, and the next statement failed on a column that was not there. Same class as `approved_users`: created outside migration tracking, invisible to a static replay, which can only tell you no migration creates a table and not whether one exists. `20260915000003_risk_data.sql` now both builds it on a fresh database and ADOPTS the one already there — renaming the quoted columns, adding the provenance columns, and marking the pre-contract rows `source: 'unrecorded (loaded before the reference-tier contract)'` rather than inventing a publisher for them. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. Capacity is what the supplier CAN ship, not what they HAVE shipped. user_ai_permissions.note: The empty-array-means-everything rule in `allowed_model_ids` is the one thing a reader of this table must not get wrong. It is deliberate — it preserves the pre-column behaviour for every user who has no row — but it inverts the usual reading of an allow-list, and nothing at the point of display says so (§5 T2).

user_capabilities.grain: One grant or denial, for one user_id and one capability. The INNERMOST layer: an explicit per-person answer that beats every other.

governance.note: One of the four layers `capabilities_for_user()` resolves, in the order role -> org -> project -> user, most specific winning. `audited: false` and it matters here more than on most tables: these rows ARE the permissions, and a change to one currently leaves no record of who made it (§2.1 `audit-actor`, WP 2.3).

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: the user the row grants for.

columns.name: capability_key
columns.meaning: The capability, naming a row in `capabilities`.

columns.name: allowed
columns.meaning: Whether this layer grants the capability. TRI-STATE in effect: a missing row means "inherit from the next layer out", `false` means "deny here". They are different answers and the resolver's COALESCE depends on the difference.

substitutions.when: no row exists at this layer
substitutions.value: the next layer out decides; the chain ends in false
substitutions.visible_as: capabilities_for_user returns the resolved boolean; which layer decided is not reported
